thesis.question: Which system should own each fact a shopper reads before buying (the product's description, its price, a discount, its stock status), and how should each fact reach the channels and the search results that show it?
thesis.claim: The four facts need four owners, not one catalog, because they do not change together (content changes by the season, a price by the day, a discount with each cart, stock by the second): product content is owned attribute by attribute in the system where its producing team works, a price by the system whose rule selects it, a discount by the cart that computes it, and stock status by one service that derives it from counted stock and commitments. A channel that can ask the owner at the moment of sale asks it; the search index and every other channel receive a copy of each fact, and a copy is safe to show only if it names its source and is compared with that source on a schedule set by how fast the fact changes.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the catalog is one record in one product, the shop platform or a product information system, which holds description, price, discount and stock together and pushes them to every channel on one schedule.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers four ownership questions before it buys a product information system, a pricing service, a search service or a faster connector, and adds a comparison of copy against source to every feed it keeps; Kestrel & Pine's Price Drift ran for nine days, and its Black Friday Oversell for an evening, because no such comparison existed.
thesis.how_why: A description may be a day old without harm, a price that is a day old is charged to real orders, a discount depends on a cart that does not exist until the shopper builds it, and the last unit can be sold in seconds; one update schedule is therefore too slow for stock or needlessly strict for content. A channel that holds its own listing cannot ask the owner at the moment of sale, so it shows a copy, and a pushed update that is lost raises no error anywhere: only a comparison finds it.

supporting_claims.claim: Product data needs one owning system per attribute, not per product, and identifiers (SKU, GTIN) that are never changed or reused, because orders, warehouses and marketplaces are keyed on them.
A price is selected from several valid candidates by one written rule, once, at order placement, and frozen on the order; the invoice and any refund copy that frozen price.

A discount is computed once, in the cart, in a declared order of evaluation with a stop rule, and is finished only when it is allocated to the order lines that invoices and refunds read; gift cards and loyalty points are balances the merchant owes, not discounts.
The search index owns no fact: it is a copy of product, price, availability and review data, so what a shopper can find is decided by what is fed into the index and how fresh each feed is.
'In stock' is a number derived from counted stock and commitments, each with one writer; it is computed in one place and published to the channels, not stored as a fact by each of them.
A channel that cannot ask the owning system at the moment of sale shows a copy, and a copy is safe to show only with a named source and a scheduled comparison against it.

flow.rationale: The page opens on one product page as the hook, to which the closing returns, and then narrows: from the part's claim about the facts on that page, to the place of those facts in one order (Eva's, before she adds the jacket to her cart), to the one company whose disagreements between copies open the chapters, to the five questions the part asks, to one paragraph per chapter; it ends on what the five answers add up to and where to start. The claim stands directly after the hook because the hook is its example; Eva's order stands before Kestrel & Pine's failures because it shows what the facts are needed for, and the failures are the cases in which one of them was wrong; (this one pair runs from a single order to the whole company, as a prerequisite step and not a narrowing: put the company first and its failures arrive before the reader knows what the facts are needed for); the five questions stand directly before the chapter list because they are the principle that orders it; the reading advice comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each one decides. Put the chapter list first and its cases (the €179 price, the Black Friday orders) arrive with no company and no claim to belong to; put the five questions before the claim and they have nothing to be questions about; put the advice first and it points at chapters the reader has not met.

hook.content: A shopper reads a jacket's description, price and stock badge on the same page. The description may stay unchanged for a season; the last sellable unit can disappear while the page is open.

bridge.from_reader_world: The shopper's side, where the description, the price and the badge sit side by side on one page.
bridge.to_topic: The merchant's side, where each of them changes at its own speed and comes from a different system, so that one update schedule cannot serve them all; and Eva's order, which needs all of them to be right before she adds the jacket to her cart on 13 April 2027.

thesis_statement.text: Under Part I's rule of one record per fact, content, price, discount and stock need four owners, not one catalog, because they change at different speeds; search owns none of them and shows copies, and a copy needs a source and a reconciliation.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS bullets 1 and 2, and paragraph p02; bullet 3 (what is promised to an order is computed once and frozen) is carried by the KEY POINTS alone and argued in the pricing, promotions and inventory chapters

promises.promise: Five chapters ask five questions in order: who owns product content and identifiers, who selects a price, how discounts combine and reach invoices and refunds, what feeds the search index, and what 'in stock' means. Each chapter opens on one Kestrel & Pine case where one fact was wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The facts a shopper reads side by side on one product page change at very different speeds, so updating them on one schedule can leave the page right about the product and wrong about whether it can be bought.

evidence.what: A jacket's page: the description may stay unchanged for a season; the last sellable unit can disappear while the page is open.
evidence.shows: Two facts on the same page with update needs so far apart that no single schedule fits both.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a product page whose description, price, discount and stock indicator connect to a season calendar, a daily calendar, a cart and a stopwatch.
evidence.shows: Four facts that sit side by side run on four different clocks, which is why each needs its own owner and its own path to every channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part II's claim: under Part I's rule of one record per fact, product content, price, discount and stock need four owners, not one catalog, because they change at different speeds; search, which owns none of them, shows copies.

evidence.what: KEY POINTS callout: catalog facts have different owners and different clocks; every channel shows a copy, and a copy needs a source and a reconciliation; a promise is computed once, in one place, and then frozen.
evidence.shows: The part's argument in three lines for a reader who skims: bullets 1 and 2 carry the owners and the copies (and that a copy needs a source and a reconciliation, which Figure 2 draws); bullet 3 (computed once, then frozen) names what the pricing, promotions and inventory chapters argue.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the shape Part II recommends: four kinds of catalog fact with four owners and four clocks, a search index (the copy of the catalog that search reads) that is openly a copy of all of them, every channel receiving those facts, and a reconciliation that compares each copy to its source on a schedule.
evidence.shows: The claim as one picture: owners on one side, copies on the other, and a comparison between them.

transition_in.carries_over: The product page whose facts change at different speeds, and Part I's rule of one record per fact (the previous page's hand-off).

sections.heading: Chapters in this part

advances_thesis.how: Each paragraph introduces the chapter that argues one of the part's supporting claims, so the list is the part's argument in outline; the pricing, search and inventory paragraphs name the comparison of copy against source that P2-6 asks for.

flow.rationale: The part's own reading order, as the journal spec declares it. Prices are stored per variant, so the product chapter's identifiers come first; a discount is subtracted from a selected price, so pricing precedes promotions; the search index is a copy of product, price and stock data, so it follows the chapters that say who owns the first two and names stock only as one of the things it copies. Availability comes last although search copies it: the stock figure the index shows is the question the search chapter leaves open, and the inventory chapter's last step, committing one unit to one order at checkout, is where Part III begins. Put inventory fourth and that one forward reference goes, but the part then ends on search and not on the unit committed at checkout. Move search first and a copy is described before the reader knows what it copies; move inventory before pricing and the price-to-discount sequence is cut in two.

transition_in.introduces: One paragraph per chapter: the question in bold, the Kestrel & Pine case it opens on and what the chapter does about it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The product chapter decides which system owns product content and identifiers: a season entered four times motivates a product information management system (PIM), and the chapter separates products, variants, stock codes and barcode identifiers.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that assigns product data to owners and fixes the identifiers.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's season entered four times by four teams (fictional).
evidence.shows: With no owner for product content, each system keeps its own version, which is the case for a product information management system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pricing chapter decides who selects a price and how channels receive it: a failed update left the German storefront at €179 instead of €199 for nine days, losing about €8,200, and start dates on prices and copy-to-source comparisons fix it.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter on price selection and names the comparison that would have found the stale copy.

evidence.what: The German storefront at €179 for nine days instead of €199, losing about €8,200 (fictional).
evidence.shows: A price copy that nothing compared with its source was charged to real orders for nine days.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter list's pattern (one chapter, one decision, signalled by 'decides') and the product the chapter before identified.
transition_in.introduces: The price each variant carries: who selects it and how channels receive it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The promotions chapter decides how offers combine and how discounts reach invoices and refunds: a leftover campaign setting let two discounts combine on 2,860 Black Friday orders at a cost of about €52,000; gift-card and loyalty balances are kept apart from discounts.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter on computing a discount once and carrying it to invoices and refunds.

evidence.what: A setting changed for one campaign and never reverted let two discounts combine on 2,860 Black Friday orders, costing about €52,000 in all, about €3,000 of it in refunds at the wrong amount (fictional).
evidence.shows: How offers combine is a setting someone must own; left as an old campaign set it, it cost about €52,000.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter list's pattern ('decides') and the price the pricing chapter selects.
transition_in.introduces: What is subtracted from that price, and how the result reaches invoices and refunds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The search chapter treats the search index as a maintained copy of product, price, stock and review data: missing attributes and synonyms hid a waterproof jacket, and fixing them, not the engine, improves results.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter that shows a copy is only as good as what is fed into it.

evidence.what: A waterproof jacket that searches could not find because attributes and synonyms were missing (fictional).
evidence.shows: The fault was in the data fed to the index, not in the search engine.

transition_in.carries_over: Product content, price and discount, each with an owner; the turn is carried by 'a maintained copy'.
transition_in.introduces: A system that holds copies of all of them: the search index, a maintained copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The inventory chapter distinguishes physical stock from what a channel may still sell: the Black Friday oversell of 1,340 jackets on storefronts and marketplaces shows what delayed copies cost, and the remedy derives availability from stock and commitments (units promised to orders), each with one owner.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the chapter on the fastest-changing fact, where a delayed copy costs most.

evidence.what: The Black Friday oversell of 1,340 jackets (fictional).
evidence.shows: Channels sold from delayed copies of a stock figure after the warehouse had none.

transition_in.carries_over: The four chapters before it, ending on the search index that copies stock.
transition_in.introduces: The last and fastest-changing fact, stock, and what 'in stock' means.

conclusion.heading: What the Five Answers Add Up To, and Where to Begin
conclusion.synthesis: The five chapters are one account of the page the part opened on: each fact on it gets an owner, and each copy a source to check it against.
conclusion.so_what: When a page is wrong, the reader first asks which fact is wrong and who owns it.

callback.to: The opening's product page (p01), where a jacket's description, price and stock badge sit side by side.
callback.how: The reader sees the opening page as separate facts, each with an owner.

hand_off.carries_over: The part's claim that the facts on one product page have different owners and change at different speeds.
hand_off.introduces: The slowest-changing of them, product content, and the identifiers on which every other catalog fact is keyed.

transition_in.carries_over: The five chapters and what each decides.
transition_in.introduces: What the five answers amount to together, seen on the opening page, and where to begin.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The answers give each fact on the opening page an owner and each copy a source, so a reader faced with a wrong page asks which fact is wrong and who owns it, and begins the part with product information.

non_goals.topic: Teaching the product model, price selection, promotion stacking, indexing or availability arithmetic; the page summarizes and does not re-argue.
Scale-stage comparisons (each chapter has its own table).
The part's closing (what the five cases have in common, read back from the end of the part).
External factual claims; the page makes none of its own.
